clue.text: Break in by levering-how resourceful!

parts.note: to break in is to enter a building by force
levering something open is prising it, using a bar as a lever

explanation.surface: An admiring exclamation at a burglar who cleverly levers his way into a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how' is a link to the exclamatory definition: the whole picture praises the burglar's ingenuity.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone enterprising shows initiative and ingenuity, which is being resourceful.

clue.text: Coats for seal-men made up?

indicators.note: made up suggests something put together or fabricated, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A question whether coats for men who hunt seals were fabricated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' reworks the seven letters of SEALMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a glossy layer applied over a surface, so enamels are coatings.

clue.text: They admit blame for hospital treatment

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one word takes another inside it

parts.note: taken as written
a rap is blame or punishment, as in taking the rap

explanation.surface: People own up to responsibility over the care given in a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admit' looks like confessing, but it means letting in; 'take the rap' is to accept blame.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is remedial care of illness, the treatment given in hospitals and clinics.

clue.text: One delivering milk and sandwiches to a chap?

parts.note: a round is a sandwich made from two whole slices of bread
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A milkman who also brings lunchtime sandwiches to a fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: A round is a British term for a sandwich of two full slices. A roundsman is a tradesman who calls on a regular route.
explanation.definitionFit: A roundsman makes regular deliveries along a route, the classic British example being the milkman.

clue.text: Hazards of a run on broken skis?

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: broken skis are smashed out of shape, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking about the dangers of skiing a run on damaged skis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' supplies the anagram of the skis; R for run is a cricket scoring convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Risks are chances of harm, the same as hazards or dangers.

clue.text: Sister holds large-sized piece of embroidery

indicators.note: holds means one piece contains another within it

parts.note: ample means large or generous in size

explanation.surface: A nun keeping hold of a big sewn needlework piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' signals the container; a sampler was traditionally stitched by girls to show off their skill.
explanation.definitionFit: A sampler is an embroidered cloth showing a range of stitches, a classic piece of needlework.

clue.text: Tars comprehensively reduced in pipe-tobacco

parts.note: tars are sailors, and all of them taken together form the navy
something reduced has been cut

explanation.surface: Sailors cut back severely on their pipe tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: Navy Cut is a traditional brand style of pressed, sliced pipe tobacco, long associated with sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Navy Cut is a type of tobacco pressed into cakes and sliced, smoked in pipes.

clue.text: What makes Ribston prosper?

parts.note: Ribston is an old apple variety (the Ribston Pippin), and to prosper is to bloom or flower, so this asks for an apple flourishing

explanation.surface: A question about what brings success to a place called Ribston.
explanation.walkthrough: Ribston looks like a village or person, but the Ribston Pippin is an English apple; prosper means bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Blossom is the spring flowering of fruit trees, here that of the apple, which is how an apple tree flourishes.

clue.text: Up late, wandering round a table-land

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one piece goes about the other
wandering means roaming aimlessly, so these letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: Staying up late and roaming about a high flat region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' rearranges UPLATE into PLATEU, which goes 'round' A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is an area of high, level ground, also called a tableland.

clue.text: Red-hot water heater, say?

parts.note: Red here means Russian, as in Soviet communism, so this is a Russian device for heating water

explanation.surface: A heater for water that glows red with heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks like a colour describing the heat, but it is the old slang for Soviet or Russian.
explanation.definitionFit: A samovar is a Russian metal urn used to boil water for tea.

clue.text: Not a single cruet trinket broken

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters are put back together differently

explanation.surface: Every one of the condiment set and little ornament got smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges CRUETTRINKET. 'Not a single' reads as 'not one', but a single is a one-way ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: A return is a there-and-back fare, the opposite of a one-way ticket, called a single in Britain.

clue.text: General keeping these islands?

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War
ward means guarding or custody, as in to keep someone in ward

explanation.surface: A military commander holding on to a group of islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: the Leeward Islands are a Caribbean chain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leeward Islands are a group in the Lesser Antilles of the Caribbean, sheltered from the prevailing wind.

clue.text: Petition is therefore lawful

parts.note: so means therefore or consequently
licit means permitted by law

explanation.surface: A statement that a petition is legally allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: To petition is to ask formally or plead, which is what soliciting means.

clue.text: Active around Beachy Head in a tall hat

indicators.note: around means one piece encircles the other

parts.note: busy means active or occupied

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone energetic walking around the cliffs of Beachy Head wearing a tall hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Beachy Head is a chalk headland on the Sussex coast; here 'Head' takes the first letter of 'Beachy', B, which goes inside BUSY.
explanation.definitionFit: A busby is a tall fur hat worn by some British soldiers, such as hussars and guards.

clue.text: Presbyterian minister who appeases

definitions.meaning: the minister who presides over a Presbyterian church court
one who calms or tempers disputes

explanation.surface: A churchman described as a peacemaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The presiding officer of a Presbyterian assembly holds this title, and in everyday use it also means a person who settles or tones down conflict.

clue.text: Leave one's craft behind

parts.note: craft here means a boat or ship, and stepping off it is leaving it behind

explanation.surface: Someone abandoning their trade or skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' suggests a skill or trade, but it is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To disembark is to get off a ship or aircraft at the end of a journey.

clue.text: Materials for portrait of a good-looker?

definitions.text: Materials for portrait of a good-looker?

parts.words: Materials for portrait of a good-looker?
parts.note: an attractive person is jokingly called an oil painting in British slang, so the materials for one are what an artist uses in oils

explanation.surface: Asking what an artist uses to paint a handsome subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She's no oil painting' is a British way of saying someone is unattractive, so a good-looker is an oil painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paints are pigments mixed with oil, the medium artists use for oil paintings.

clue.text: Lamb, under a high ball, makes a bloomer

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece under another comes after it

parts.note: a lob is a ball hit high into the air
Charles Lamb wrote essays under the pen name Elia

explanation.surface: A lamb under a lofted ball causes a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' looks like a mistake but is a flowering plant; Lamb is the essayist Charles Lamb, whose pen name was Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobelia is a garden plant grown for its blue flowers, so it is a flower-bearer.

clue.text: Very silly, like 19 say?

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons
the number 19 spoken digit by digit is one, nine, giving I (Roman one) and nine

explanation.surface: A description of something foolish, comparing it to clue 19.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is a trick: 19 is read as its digits, 1 (Roman I) and 9 (NINE), not as another answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means extremely stupid, literally like a donkey.

clue.text: Course for Robert Burns, for example

definitions.meaning: a racecourse, the Berkshire track famous for Royal ...
the poet Robert Burns is a native of Scotland, read here as two words, a Scot

explanation.surface: A racecourse picked for the Scottish poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as two words, A SCOT; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a racecourse, the scene of the Royal Ascot meeting.

clue.text: A ship, for example, equipped with first-class weapon

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
A1 (here AI) means first-class, from Lloyd's register of ships

explanation.surface: A vessel armed with a top-quality weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is written AI, the digit 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: An assegai is a slender spear used by peoples of southern Africa.

clue.text: I have supported American state in plot

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that supports another sits beneath it

parts.note: Conn. is an abbreviation for Connecticut
I have contracts to I've

explanation.surface: Someone claiming to have backed a US state in a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supported' puts IVE below CONN in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To connive is to conspire or scheme secretly, which is to plot.

clue.text: Heavenly, under tree!

parts.note: sub is Latin for under
the lime is a tree, also called the linden

explanation.surface: An exclamation of bliss at lying beneath a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Sublime means of supreme excellence or beauty, wonderful as heaven.

clue.text: Upright characters in the rectory

indicators.note: the characters are the letters within these words, so the answer sits among them

explanation.surface: Morally upright figures living in a vicarage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' suggests people in the rectory, but it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means standing straight up, which is upright.

clue.text: Motorway casino turned into a sort of lodge

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

indicators.note: turned into suggests a change of form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A roadside gambling hall converted into a meeting hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned into' is the anagram signal, not a link to the definition; the Freemasons meet in lodges.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasons meet in Masonic lodges, so this word describes a kind of lodge.

clue.text: Angst is a male disturbance!

indicators.note: a disturbance is an upheaval, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A statement that anxiety is a male upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbance' rearranges ISAMALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaise is a vague feeling of unease or discomfort, close to angst or anxiety.

clue.text: Viewpoint about last Gaelic couple in English

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: an angle is a point of view on something
the last pair of letters in Gaelic are I and C

explanation.surface: A perspective on the last Gaelic pair translated into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the container; 'last Gaelic couple' takes the final two letters of the word Gaelic.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglice is a Latin adverb used in English texts to mean in the English language.

clue.text: Means to get 16 on the canvas?

definitions.text: Means to get 16 on the canvas?

parts.words: Means to get 16 on the canvas?
parts.note: 16 refers to the artist's paints, and the tool asked for spreads them on a canvas; canvas also suggests a boxing ring

explanation.surface: Asking how to knock someone down onto the boxing ring floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the canvas' hints at boxing, but it is a painting surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A palette knife is a thin flexible blade artists use to mix and apply paint.
